findings.claim: AO3 (context) is worth 4 of the 34 marks on the Shakespeare question
findings.truth: AO3 is worth 6 marks. The Shakespeare question is 30 marks plus 4 separate spelling, punctuation and grammar marks, split AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6. The '4 marks' the lesson names are the SPaG marks, not context.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, weighting table (Paper 1: AO1 15%, AO2 15%, AO3 7.5%, AO4 2.5% of a 40% / 64-mark component). Confirmed against this unit's own L7 conclusion: 'AO1 + AO2 ... are worth 24 of 34 marks'.

findings.claim: commonwealth: 'an imagined perfect society ... from Thomas More's 1516 book of the same name'
findings.truth: More's 1516 book is Utopia. He wrote no book called Commonwealth, so 'of the same name' is false.

findings.claim: '... Which thou forget'st.' (actual line: Prospero must remind Ariel of her own history because Ariel tends to forget it - not that Ariel acknowledges a monthly debt to Prospero)
findings.truth: An earlier editor's correction note was left inside the live lesson text, in brackets, contradicting the sentence it follows. Prospero's line means he has to retell Ariel's own history once a month because Ariel forgets it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042, 1.2: 'I must / Once in a month recount what thou hast been, / Which thou forget'st.' (Prospero, before recounting Sycorax and the cloven pine).

findings.claim: 'No one is harmed, as Prospero later confirms: "Not a hair perished."' (repeated on flashcard 4)
findings.truth: Ariel says the line, answering Prospero's question. Prospero asks; Ariel reports.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042, 1.2: '_Pros._ But are they, Ariel, safe? / _Ari._ Not a hair perish'd'.

findings.claim: Caliban: 'The son of the dead witch Sycorax and the devil Setebos'
findings.truth: Setebos is the god Sycorax worshipped, not Caliban's father. Caliban's father is an unnamed devil. The lesson body already corrects this; the glossary still carried the wrong version, so the two contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042, 1.2: Caliban, 'It would control my dam's god, Setebos'; Prospero, 'Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself'.

findings.claim: Practice question 4 in EVERY lesson (1-7) is labelled '30 marks - Essay'.
findings.truth: Its own mark scheme runs Top band (11-12), Upper band (9-10), (7-8), (5-6), (3-4), (1-2) - a 12-mark ladder. The genuine 30+4 Shakespeare task is already question 5 in each lesson. Relabelled '12 marks - Essay'; the mark scheme is untouched.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction between the question type and its own band ladder; AQA has no 30-mark scheme topping out at 12.

findings.claim: servitude: 'Voluntary submission to another person's authority or wishes'
findings.truth: Servitude means being under another's control and bound to serve. Defining it as voluntary reverses the lesson's own point, which is that Ferdinand chooses service while Caliban and Ariel do not.
findings.evidence: Standard sense of the word; contradicted by the same paragraph ('contrasts sharply with Caliban's forced labour').

findings.claim: The epilogue is unique in Shakespeare.
findings.truth: Shakespeare wrote several epilogues. Puck's epilogue to A Midsummer Night's Dream also asks the audience for pardon and applause. What is unusual here is that the character who has just surrendered his magic asks for release.
findings.evidence: A Midsummer Night's Dream, As You Like It, Henry V, 2 Henry IV, All's Well That Ends Well all carry epilogues.

findings.field: content_html, exam_tip_html, flashcard_questions, practice_questions (also L3 practice_questions)
findings.claim: 'Prospero and Miranda call him a "thing of darkness," a "monster," and "a born devil"' (and four more places attributing 'monster' to Prospero)
findings.truth: 'Monster' is only ever spoken by Stephano and Trinculo. Prospero uses 'thing of darkness' (5.1) and 'a born devil' (4.1). Miranda uses none of the three. A student quoting 'monster' as Prospero's word would be wrong on the text.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042: every occurrence of 'monster' about Caliban is Stephano's or Trinculo's (2.2, 3.2, 4.1, 5.1 'bully-monster'). Antonio's 'a monster's ear' (2.1) is not about Caliban.

findings.claim: The 12-mark ladder on question 4 names two different bands 'Top band' (11-12 and 7-8), in all seven lessons.
findings.truth: Cosmetic. The mark ranges are correct and unambiguous, so a student self-marking is not misled. Left alone to keep the edit surgical.

findings.claim: 'For the exam , this speech is crucial' - stray space before the comma.
findings.truth: A typo, not a factual error. Recorded for a future copy pass.

summary: Seven lessons checked against the Gutenberg text and the spec. Four HIGH findings: an AO3 mark claim that contradicts the spec and the unit's own L7 conclusion, an editor's correction note left in live lesson text, 'Not a hair perished' given to Prospero instead of Ariel, and a glossary entry naming Setebos as Caliban's father. Five MEDIUM findings, including 'monster' attributed to Prospero in five places and a '30 marks' label on a question whose own mark scheme tops out at 12 (all seven lessons). Lessons 6 and 7 carry only that shared label fix.
